\subsection{Member 2: Abdul Raffay}
\textbf{What I built.} I own the \path{runner/} package and \path{.github/}, and I am the integration owner. I built the order runner and its JUnit harness (W6), the diagnosis runs: victim-alone check, polluter search, repeated runs, source integrity and the execution record (W7), the command \texttt{py -m runner diagnose} that joins the three packages (W9, with Member 3's report assembly), minimisation with \texttt{ddmin} (W10), and the given and shuffled orders with honest \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED} reports (W14). I also restructured the code and documentation into one repository with CI and the team rules (W5, \pr{1}), wrote ADR-003, 004, 005, 007 and 008, and set up and compiled this report. On \texttt{main} that is 22 merged pull requests and 78 commits, 18 of them for the report (Table~\ref{ch9:tab:git}); Section~\ref{ch6:sec:m2} describes the module.

\textbf{Reviews.} Like every member, I reviewed pull requests I did not write. Four problems I found in Member 3's report assembly are recorded in its code as ``flagged by Member 2'' (\path{eval/report.py}): evidence requested at depth 1, which cannot see F2's property read one call below the test; a generic ``no edge was found'' line that contradicted the evidence for several polluters; a merge order in which the command would crash instead of exiting with code 3; and report text that said ``given order'' when no order was given.

\textbf{One decision: what to do when a failure does not reproduce (ADR-008).} At first, a victim that never failed in 20 runs of its order ended with exit code 3 and no report. That was wrong in two ways. The order we ran was the one we discovered, alphabetical, not the one that failed in CI, so 20 repetitions of it might never reproduce a real order-dependent failure. And a clean run proves nothing about the test, because no number of reruns can show that a test is reliable. I decided that FlakeTrace should accept the real failing order (\texttt{-{}-order}), try up to 31 distinct shuffled orders when nothing fails, always run the victim alone, and then write an honest \texttt{NOT\_REPRODUCED} report that says what was tried and gives the statistical bound, never ``the test is fine''. I rejected reusing Member 3's random-order baseline for the shuffling, because FlakeTrace is evaluated against that baseline and must stay independent of it. The result on the fixture: F4, which the discovered order never reproduces, is \texttt{VERIFIED} through the second shuffled order (seed 1), and N3 gets a report with the bound ``failure rate below 0.161''. The cost is up to 71 JVM runs for a victim that never fails.

\textbf{One limitation of my module.} Each test method runs as its own JUnit request, so a class's \texttt{@BeforeClass} and \texttt{@AfterClass} run once per method instead of once per class as under Maven Surefire. A test that depends on that class-level setup running only once may behave differently under FlakeTrace than under Maven. Fixing it means grouping consecutive methods of one class into one request without changing the order; it is not needed for the fixture, and I have not done it yet.
